# SK0234 — The cast or type argument is redundant

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A cast whose operand already has the cast's type, explicit method type arguments inference reproduces exactly, an array size that repeats the element count, and tuple component names the declared type already carries.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Cleanup |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

Each one is a conversion that converts nothing, and each is read as if it might. A cast makes a reader ask what the operand was before it; explicit type arguments make them ask what inference would have chosen; an array size makes them count the elements to see whether the two agree.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var name = (string)text;
var items = Enumerable.Empty<int>().ToList<int>();
var row = new string[2] { "a", "b" };
(string Name, int Age) person = (Name: name, Age: 30);
```

Write:

```csharp
var name = text;
var items = Enumerable.Empty<int>().ToList();
var row = new string[] { "a", "b" };
(string Name, int Age) person = (name, 30);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A cast is not redundant merely because the types allow removing it, and this rule is written around that sentence.** `var x = (long)1;` types `x` as `long` and `var x = 1;` types it as `int`. `M((object)s)` and `M(s)` call different overloads. `flag ? (long)a : b` infers a different type once the cast is gone. Roslyn's own `IDE0004` is the standing example of getting this wrong, so Skala covers the one subset where none of those questions can be asked: an **identity** conversion, where the operand's type and the cast's type are the same symbol — checked with `SymbolEqualityComparer.IncludeNullability` and confirmed by `ClassifyConversion(...).IsIdentity`. The expression's type is then unchanged by the deletion, so nothing downstream of it can change either. ⚠ **Every widening, narrowing and boxing cast is therefore deliberately uncovered**, including the upcast that is most of what `RedundantCast` reports in practice. That is a smaller rule on purpose; the negative fixture set records each declined shape. ⚠ Nullability is not a detail here: `(string)maybeNull` is typed `string` where its operand is `string?`, so the cast is what tells the flow analysis what the author knows, and a `var` declared from it would change type without it. ⚠ Tuples are excluded from the cast branch entirely and handled by the component-name branch, because `((int a, int b))(1, 2)` and `((int, int))(1, 2)` differ in the names the result carries. ⚠ Explicit method type arguments are removed only where re-binding the call without them reaches the **identical constructed method** — the same definition with different inferred type arguments does not count. ⚠ An array size is matched for one dimension only: a jagged or rectangular creation has sizes whose relationship to the initializer is not the flat count this compares against. ⚠ Tuple component names are dropped only under a **written** tuple type. Under `var` the names come from the literal and deleting them deletes them from the variable's type, and no semantic query separates those two cases because the resulting type is identical. ⚠ **Four of the family's eight inspections are not covered**: `RedundantExplicitArrayCreation` (`new object[] { "a", "b" }` infers `string[]` once the type is dropped), `RedundantExplicitNullableCreation`, `RedundantTypeArgumentsInsideNameof` and `PreferExplicitlyProvidedTupleComponentName`, which asks for the opposite of what this rule does.
